performers: William McColl, basset clarinet; University of Washington Symphony Orchestra, Abraham Kaplan
question: When the soloist takes over an orchestral idea, what changes besides its tone colour?
intro: The orchestra establishes a complete conversation before the soloist takes it over. William McColl plays a basset clarinet he built himself, restoring the low-register possibilities for which Mozart wrote the concerto.

sections.label: Orchestral opening
sections.mNote: A major; themes before the solo exposition

sections.label: Solo exposition
sections.mNote: The opening theme gains a solo voice

sections.label: Development · changing ground
sections.mNote: The solo line explores contrasting tonal regions

sections.label: Recapitulation · shared return

cues.title: The orchestra speaks first
cues.text: Strings introduce the opening melody over a moving inner pulse. The soloist’s first independent statement comes later: listen now for the melodic shapes that will become part of the clarinet’s vocabulary.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf score (1881), I, PDF pp. 1–5, labelled opening Tutti and later Solo. Report begins quietly, then gains relative level through 0:15–0:35. No claim is made about optional solo doubling in the tutti.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Running lines and chords
cues.text: The opening paragraph alternates broad chords with running figures. Flutes and violins can share the quick movement while the lower strings keep it connected to a firm bass line.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf I, opening orchestral ritornello, PDF pp. 1–4; report rises to −7.8 dB at 0:35 with increased onset density. This is a passage description.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Remember more than a tune
cues.text: Try to remember the orchestra’s ways of answering as well as its melodies. Imitation and small echoing phrases will remain useful when the solo clarinet becomes the centre of attention.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf I, opening ritornello, PDF pp. 2–5; report alternates stronger 1:05–1:10 and quieter 1:15–1:20 windows. No particular imitative entry is timed.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: A new speaking voice
cues.text: The solo exposition gives the opening idea to the clarinet, with a lighter orchestral background. A familiar melody becomes more flexible when one player can extend it with runs, turns and changes of register.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf I, first Solo on PDF p. 5, bar 57; report falls from −8.6 dB at 1:35 to −20.4 dB at 1:40 and −24.2 dB at 1:45. The solo-entry marker at 1:40 is provisional.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Written for Stadler
cues.text: Mozart writes the concerto for Anton Stadler, whose instrument extends below the range of an ordinary clarinet. That lower register is part of the work’s design, not a later decorative addition.
cues.evidence: Calvin Dotsey, Houston Symphony, “Swan Song: Mozart’s Clarinet Concerto”, https://houstonsymphony.org/swan-song-mozarts-clarinet-concerto/.
cues.how: Documented fact.

cues.title: Major gives way to shadow
cues.text: In this part of the solo exposition, the initially secure major-key world becomes less stable. Follow the line through its darker turns rather than treating every change of register as a new theme.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf I, solo exposition, PDF pp. 7–9; report boundaries 2:42 and 2:48 accompany departure from the opening A-major profile. The score, not the local-key estimator, establishes the minor-mode contrast.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Breath and long phrases
cues.text: Listen for how the solo line makes several small gestures into one longer phrase. An instrumental melody need not stop wherever a singer would need to breathe, but this concerto often invites that comparison.
cues.evidence: Score I, solo exposition, PDF pp. 8–11; report 3:30–3:50 remains at moderate relative level with the dominant region becoming more stable. This is a listening strategy, not a measured breath.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: A lost autograph
cues.text: The concerto’s complete autograph does not survive. Early printed versions adapt the solo part for the ordinary clarinet, so modern basset-clarinet performances must reconstruct details of the lost low-register writing.
cues.evidence: Calvin Dotsey, Houston Symphony, “Swan Song: Mozart’s Clarinet Concerto”, https://houstonsymphony.org/swan-song-mozarts-clarinet-concerto/.
cues.how: Documented fact.

cues.title: Not always in front
cues.text: The clarinet can support an orchestral melody with broken-chord movement rather than continually carrying the tune. Listen for moments when the apparent soloist behaves like an accompanist.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf I, later solo exposition, PDF pp. 11–13; report returns to a sustained E-major profile from 4:35–5:05 after the low-level 4:25 window. The role reversal is from the score and is not assigned to an exact bar here.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The orchestra closes a paragraph
cues.text: The orchestral ritornello gathers the exposition’s material into a firmer conclusion. Its fuller texture is a structural landmark, but it does not mean that the concerto has finished its argument.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf I, Tutti on PDF pp. 13–14; report rises from −15.6 dB at 5:15 to −8.4 dB at 5:20 and remains strong through 5:35.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A busy final autumn
cues.text: The concerto belongs to the same final autumn as The Magic Flute and La clemenza di Tito. Mozart is still writing for particular performers and institutions; the music need not be read as a coded farewell.
cues.evidence: Composer biography, 1791; Calvin Dotsey, Houston Symphony, “Swan Song: Mozart’s Clarinet Concerto”, https://houstonsymphony.org/swan-song-mozarts-clarinet-concerto/.
cues.how: Documented fact.

cues.title: Familiar shapes travel
cues.text: The development draws the clarinet through changing tonal surroundings. Fragments of the opening vocabulary remain recognisable even when the bass no longer gives them the same harmonic support.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf I, development, PDF pp. 14–18; report boundaries 6:26 and 6:32 precede changing pitch profiles and contrasting relative levels around 6:35–6:50.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Colour inside the line
cues.text: Through the central passage, follow the solo line as it crosses registers. McColl’s extended instrument allows a low response to belong to the same musical sentence as a much brighter upper phrase.
cues.evidence: The basset instrument is documented by the performer archive. Report boundary 7:06 and changing pitch profiles support the central contrasting passage, but no particular reconstructed low note is located.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: The player builds the instrument
cues.text: The performer archive identifies McColl’s basset clarinet as an instrument of his own construction. It does not identify the reconstruction or edition of the solo part, so the guide leaves that question open.
cues.evidence: Wikimedia Commons file description and Soni Ventorum archive, Mozart K. 622, https://soniventorum.com/soniventorum_archives.html.
cues.how: Documented fact.

cues.title: The ensemble gathers again
cues.text: The orchestra’s fuller writing prepares the return from the development. Listen for the solo line’s changing relationship to a texture that can now speak collectively again.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf I, final developmental tutti and return preparation, PDF pp. 18–20; report boundaries 7:56 and 8:08, with higher relative level at 8:10–8:20.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The opening returns together
cues.text: The recapitulatory passage restores the opening material to A major. Soloist and orchestra now revisit a shared history: the theme no longer sounds like something one side has introduced to the other for the first time.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf I, Solo and returning main theme, PDF pp. 20–21; report turns quieter at 8:30–8:35 and remains strongly A-major centred through 9:10. Section marker 8:30 is provisional.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A shadow within the return
cues.text: The return does not simply erase the minor-mode material. Listen for darker turns inside the home-key passage before the line again finds its major-key balance.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf I, recapitulated solo exposition, PDF pp. 22–24; report boundary 9:18 and A-minor-centred windows around 9:20–9:25 corroborate the score’s local modal contrast.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Follow the answering strings
cues.text: The strings are more than a quiet surface underneath the soloist. Try following one of their answering figures for a phrase, then return your attention to the clarinet and hear how the two lines fit.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf I, recapitulation, PDF pp. 23–26; report has boundary 9:52 and moderate, varied relative level across 9:55–10:15. This is a general listening task.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: A university performance
cues.text: McColl plays with the University of Washington Symphony Orchestra under Abraham Kaplan in December 1987. The sources identify the month and ensemble, but not a particular day or concert hall.
cues.evidence: Wikimedia Commons file description and Soni Ventorum archive, Mozart K. 622, https://soniventorum.com/soniventorum_archives.html.
cues.how: Documented fact.

cues.title: Motion without a new destination
cues.text: The later solo passage revisits quick figures and answering orchestral material within the home-key argument. Listen for increasing continuity rather than expecting another large change of scene.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf I, late recapitulation, PDF pp. 26–28; after the low-level 10:50 window, the report resumes an A-major profile across 11:05–11:25.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The orchestra has the last word
cues.text: The final orchestral ritornello takes over the close. Its firm phrases answer the soloist’s more elaborate movement without requiring a long, separate showpiece cadenza.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf I, final Tutti, PDF pp. 28–29; report rises from −15.8 dB at 11:40 to −7.8 dB at 11:45. The 11:44 section marker is a passage estimate, not a timed entry.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A clear full stop
cues.text: The final A-major cadence closes the first movement. Listen for the distinction between the last musical chord and the quieter recording tail that follows it.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf I, final page 29; report falls from −12.8 dB at 12:15 to −43.8 dB at 12:20 and −50.2 dB at 12:25. The cue describes the ending span rather than an exact cutoff.
cues.how: Located by measuring this recording.

transitions.title: The tutti yields the theme
transitions.how: The opening orchestral ritornello closes firmly in A major. The accompaniment thins and the clarinet takes up the main melody, extending it with soloistic decoration. A cadence and a change of texture mark the new formal role without requiring a new key.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf I, first Solo, PDF p. 5; report relative-level fall around 1:40–1:45.

transitions.title: The dominant close opens outward
transitions.how: The exposition’s orchestral close establishes E major. The clarinet resumes with familiar material, but the continuation carries it into contrasting tonal regions rather than merely repeating the exposition. The opening idea supplies the link while changing harmony gives it a new function.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf I, end of orchestral ritornello and development opening, PDF pp. 14–15; report E-major region through 6:20, followed by stronger boundaries at 6:26–6:48. The marker estimates the earlier solo restart, not a detected key change.

transitions.title: The home key receives the soloist
transitions.how: Sequential orchestral writing and dominant preparation lead back to A major. The soloist returns to the opening melody over a lighter accompaniment. Familiar material now continues towards the tonic rather than retracing the exposition’s move to E major.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf I, PDF pp. 19–21; report fuller 8:10–8:25 span and reduction around 8:30–8:35. Timing remains provisional.

transitions.title: Solo movement becomes ensemble closure
transitions.how: The solo line brings its quick passagework to a cadence, and the orchestra gathers the closing material into A major. Winds and horns strengthen the string texture. The movement ends through the return of an established orchestral function, not through a new thematic episode.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf I, PDF pp. 28–29; report sharp relative-level rise at 11:45 and sustained stronger windows through 11:55.

source.title: Mozart, Clarinet Concerto K. 622, Breitkopf & Härtel, Mozarts Werke XII/20 (1881), plate W.A.M. 622; shared orchestral fabric only

composer.epithet: An opera composer whose instrumental music gives different voices the freedom to disagree.
facts: By his father Leopold; extensive performing tours from childhood
Salzburg · Italy · Mannheim and Paris · Vienna from 1781
Italian opera seria and opera buffa; German Singspiel with spoken dialogue
K. or KV = Ludwig von Köchel’s catalogue, first published in 1862 and repeatedly revised
composer.background:
Mozart was born in Salzburg in 1756, the seventh child of Leopold Mozart and Anna Maria Pertl; only he and his sister Maria Anna survived infancy. Leopold was a violinist and composer in the archbishop’s service, and in the year of Wolfgang’s birth published an influential violin treatise. He taught both children. Maria Anna, called Nannerl within the family, became an accomplished keyboard player, and the first tours presented brother and sister together. The family’s travels were an educational system as well as a business: the children encountered instruments, performers, repertories and audiences that a Salzburg childhood alone could not have supplied.

The long tour of 1763–66 took them through German courts, Paris, London and the Netherlands. In London Mozart met Johann Christian Bach, whose clear phrases and Italianate melodic style offered a model different from the contrapuntal teaching associated with Bach’s father. Illness repeatedly interrupted the itinerary. Leopold managed engagements, publicity and money while supervising composition, and the surviving correspondence documents the costs and uncertainties behind the public demonstrations. Wolfgang learned to write for named performers and immediate occasions before he had an independent adult household.
